identity.title: Phage-directed precision microbiome medicine: engineering pathobiont depletion, synbiotic succession, microbial-function editing, metabolite host signaling, neurophagomics, and durable ecological state control in gut dysbiosis associated diseases.

content.abstract: Bacteriophages are being investigated as strain-selective tools for modifying intestinal microbial communities, but the evidence supporting ecological reconstruction is substantially less mature than the evidence supporting targeted bacterial depletion. This review separates current knowledge into three domains: established and emerging experimental evidence, human translational evidence, and hypotheses proposed for future testing. Human studies show that orally administered natural or engineered phages can be recovered from the gastrointestinal tract and can alter selected bacterial populations without antibiotic-like loss of overall community diversity. Preclinical studies further demonstrate targeted suppression of inflammatory Klebsiella pneumoniae in inflammatory bowel disease models, cytolytic Enterococcus faecalis in alcohol-associated liver disease, evolutionary steering of Escherichia coli, in situ bacterial genome editing, local therapeutic-protein production, and phage-probiotic cooperation. These findings do not yet establish that an integrated phage-successor-prebiotic sequence can durably reprogram a human gut ecosystem. To organize this translational gap, we use Subtract-Seed-Feed-Lock as an explicitly proposed design framework. A phage or phage-derived platform first depletes, weakens, or edits a disease-relevant bacterial strain or function; a niche-matched successor is then introduced; a selectively utilized nutrient supports that successor; and durability is assessed after treatment withdrawal. Related terms used in this review-Functional Phageability, Minimum Ecological Dose, Ecological Vacancy Window, nutrient-conditioned phagogram, ecological pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (Eco-PK/PD), ecological pharmacovigilance, neurophagomic reverse translation, and microbiome-state digital twin-are hypothesis-generating operational concepts rather than validated clinical methods. Host signaling is likewise framed as predominantly indirect: phage-induced changes in bacterial abundance or function may alter lipopolysaccharide, short-chain fatty acids, indoles, bile acids, and other metabolites that subsequently engage inflammatory, barrier, hepatic, or neural pathways. The gut-brain application remains especially preliminary; targeting urdA-positive imidazole-propionate producers has not been validated with therapeutic phages. Clinical development will require reproducible good manufacturing practice, control of endotoxin and host-cell contaminants, product stability, resistance and immune-neutralization monitoring, environmental-shedding assessment, and regulatory strategies for genetically modified, dynamically updated, and multi-component products. The immediate opportunity is therefore precise microbial perturbation with evidence-matched endpoints; durable programmed reconstruction remains an experimentally testable objective.
